reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: Defined by dominant or co-dominant mesangial C1q deposition on immunofluorescence in the absence of clinical and serological evidence of systemic lupus erythematosus
Occurs mainly in older children and young adults and often presents with proteinuria or nephrotic syndrome, sometimes with haematuria
Underlying light-microscopic patterns are variable, commonly minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or a proliferative picture
By definition, lupus serology (antinuclear and anti-DNA antibodies) is negative and there are no extrarenal lupus features, which separates it from lupus nephritis
Electron microscopy shows mesangial, and sometimes paramesangial, electron-dense immune-type deposits
Its status as a distinct disease versus an immunofluorescence pattern remains debated, so it is a diagnosis of careful exclusion
Treatment is guided by the underlying histology and proteinuria, using immunosuppression/corticosteroids as for the corresponding podocytopathy or proliferative lesion
reference.pathophysiology: C1q nephropathy is characterised by mesangial deposition of C1q, the recognition component of the classical complement pathway, together with immunoglobulins, forming immune-type deposits without the serological hallmarks of lupus. The mechanism is uncertain: C1q may be deposited as part of immune complexes or bind altered mesangial antigens, activating the classical pathway and provoking a variable injury response that ranges from a pure podocytopathy to mesangial or endocapillary proliferation. The resulting disturbance of the glomerular filtration barrier produces proteinuria, and more proliferative lesions add haematuria and functional decline. Because C1q deposition also features prominently in lupus nephritis, exclusion of systemic lupus is central to the definition.
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence showing dominant mesangial C1q and electron microscopy for deposits
Antinuclear and anti-double-stranded-DNA antibodies to exclude lupus
Quantification of proteinuria and assessment of renal function
Urinalysis with microscopy for haematuria and casts
Serologies to exclude infective and other immune-complex causes
redFlags: Evolving clinical or serological features of systemic lupus erythematosus
Rapidly progressive renal impairment or crescentic change on biopsy
Nephrotic syndrome with thromboembolic or infective complications
Steroid resistance suggesting an aggressive underlying lesion
reference.prognosis: Outcome largely follows the underlying histological pattern and the response of proteinuria to treatment: minimal-change-like disease may respond well, whereas focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or proliferative lesions with steroid resistance carry a higher risk of progressive renal impairment. Long-term follow-up is needed because a minority later manifest systemic lupus.
pitfalls: Diagnosing C1q nephropathy without excluding systemic lupus erythematosus
Ignoring the underlying light-microscopic lesion that guides treatment and prognosis
Over-treating a minimal-change-like course with prolonged aggressive immunosuppression
Failing to monitor for later evolution into lupus
Regarding mesangial C1q staining as diagnostic in isolation
management: Direct immunosuppression by the underlying histological pattern, using corticosteroids first-line for minimal-change-like or nephrotic presentations and calcineurin inhibitors or other agents for steroid-resistant disease or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Reduce proteinuria and control blood pressure with renin-angiotensin system blockade using an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker
Manage nephrotic-syndrome complications with sodium restriction and diuretics for oedema, treatment of dyslipidaemia, thromboprophylaxis and attention to infection risk
Confirm the diagnosis by renal biopsy and continue to exclude evolving systemic lupus with serial autoantibody testing
Monitor proteinuria, renal function, blood pressure and treatment response over time
Refer to nephrology for biopsy-based classification and prognostication
Manage progression towards chronic kidney disease and plan for renal replacement therapy if function declines
